problem:
First, decree that T(1,1) = 1. Then for n > 0, let S(n) = {(i,j) : 1 <= i <= n, 1 <= j <= n},
and let

T(1,n+1) = least positive integer not among T(i,j) for (i,j) in S(n);
T(n+1,1) = least positive integer not among T(i,j) for (i,j) in S(n) and not (T,n+1);
T(m,n+1) = T(m,1)*T(1,n+1).

These rules generate an array T which starts out like this:

T = [
    [1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 13, 15, 18, 23, 25, 29],
    [3, 6, 12, 21, 27, 39, 45, 54, 69, 75, 87],
    [5, 10, 20, 35, 45, 65, 75, 90, 115, 125, 145],
    [8, 16, 32, 56, 72, 104, 120, 144, 184, 200, 232],
    [11, 22, 44, 77, 99, 143, 165, 198, 253, 275, 319]
]

Every prime is in row 1 of T or column 1, but not both.

The difference sequence of row 1 starts with

1,2,3,2,4,2,3,5,2,4,2,5,4,2,4,3,2,4,3,2,2,4,4,7,2,3,2,4,3,5,5,3,4.

Here's the problem: prove (or disprove) that this difference sequence bounded.

More terms of the array T and its first row are given at A129258 and A129259.

framings.reframing: Treat the border construction as an endogenous mex game. At stage n, the represented integers act like the option set of a position, and b_{n+1} is the mex of that option set. The bounded-gap question becomes whether this evolving mex graph can force arbitrarily large jumps in its Grundy labels, or whether its structure enforces uniformly bounded mex increments.
framings.key_insight: This makes the problem natively about mex rather than about products. Long gaps become failures of interval completion in an option graph, which is exactly the kind of obstruction combinatorial game theory knows how to encode.
framings.suggested_technique: Build a directed option graph and import Sprague-Grundy methods: search for a monotone invariant or eventual periodicity criterion for mex values on this graph that would force mex(H_{n+1}) - mex(H_n) <= C.
framings.mapping_back: If the option sets generated by the product tableau satisfy a game-theoretic interval-closure property, then the mex values b_n inherit bounded increments, proving the original gap sequence is bounded.

framings.domain: Extremal graph theory and forbidden 0-1 matrices
framings.reframing: Encode representability by a bipartite incidence matrix or ordered 0-1 matrix whose rows are the current a_i values, columns are the current b_j values, and occupied cells represent products a_i b_j. Large jumps in b_n correspond to long zero windows adjacent to the ordered frontier of this matrix.
framings.key_insight: The problem becomes geometric: how large can an empty staircase or forbidden zero block survive next to a monotone product frontier created by a greedy update rule? That is much closer to Zarankiewicz-style and forbidden-submatrix questions than to direct divisor counting.
framings.suggested_technique: Define a forbidden matrix pattern that any long gap would create, then apply extremal 0-1 matrix bounds of Marcus-Tardos or related forbidden-submatrix machinery to show such zero windows cannot persist past a fixed size.
framings.mapping_back: A theorem ruling out arbitrarily large frontier-adjacent zero configurations would translate directly into a universal bound on the size of gaps between successive b_n.

framings.domain: Combinatorics on words and symbolic dynamics
framings.reframing: View the first-row difference sequence d_n = b_{n+1} - b_n as an infinite word over the positive integers. The open problem then asks whether this word is actually over a finite alphabet, and possibly whether it belongs to a recurrent or substitutive subshift.
framings.key_insight: This shifts attention from individual products to the global regularity of the gap word. Boundedness is equivalent to finite alphabet size, so tools about recurrence, return words, and S-adic structure become relevant immediately.
framings.suggested_technique: Look for a coding of the greedy border update as a symbolic system and then apply return-word and linear-recurrence criteria in the style of Durand to prove the gap word is uniformly recurrent over a finite alphabet.
framings.mapping_back: If the difference word can be shown to come from a linearly recurrent or substitutive system, then only finitely many gap sizes can occur, which is exactly the bounded-difference claim.

framings.reframing: Treat a_n and b_n as a nonclassical pair of complementary greedy sequences. They split arithmetic information asymmetrically, with primes landing in exactly one border, so the right question is whether they behave like an almost-Beatty or Lambek-Moser complementary pair generated by a multiplicative exclusion rule.
framings.key_insight: This reframing puts the two border sequences, not the whole table, at center stage. If either border is close to an inverse or complementary law of Beatty type, bounded first differences become a natural regularity consequence rather than a mysterious byproduct.
framings.suggested_technique: Test whether the border pair satisfies an asymptotic complementary relation and then use Lambek-Moser inverse-sequence machinery or almost-Beatty estimates to control local fluctuations of b_n.
framings.mapping_back: Any proof that b_n is an almost-Beatty sequence with uniformly bounded local error would immediately yield a uniform bound on b_{n+1} - b_n.

framings.domain: Statistical physics of exclusion processes and adsorption
framings.reframing: Interpret represented integers as occupied sites in a one-dimensional medium whose occupancy is induced by product interactions between two growing species A and B. Then b_{n+1} is the first vacancy after the current occupied block, and record gaps are unusually large vacancy islands near a moving interface.
framings.key_insight: The border is an interface-growth object. Instead of asking whether divisors are dense enough, ask whether the deterministic exclusion dynamics can sustain arbitrarily large holes near the adsorption front.
framings.suggested_technique: Borrow hard-core lattice-gas and random sequential adsorption tools such as contour arguments, transfer-matrix approximations, or cluster-expansion style vacancy estimates to model and bound the width of the frontier hole region.
framings.mapping_back: A uniform bound on interface roughness or vacancy-island width in the induced exclusion model would become a uniform bound on the first-row gaps b_{n+1} - b_n.

framings.reframing: View the construction as an online covering process on the positive integers. At each step the algorithm is forced to expose the smallest currently uncovered integer b_{n+1}, then it pays for a new row and column that cover many future integers through products.
framings.key_insight: A long gap means the process has failed to cover an interval efficiently before it was forced to open the next resource. This is exactly the language of adversarial online covering and competitive analysis.
framings.suggested_technique: Formulate interval coverage by current products as an online covering LP and apply primal-dual methods from online set cover or online covering to bound the dual mass that a long uncovered interval could accumulate.
framings.mapping_back: If each greedy update can be shown to buy enough future coverage in the primal-dual sense, then uncovered intervals of length greater than a constant cannot survive, giving bounded gaps in b_n.

framings.reframing: Pose a long-gap event as an optimization or feasibility problem: can the current border sets A_n and B_n avoid representing every integer in an interval [x, x+L]? Then the original question becomes whether there exists any feasible witness for arbitrarily large L under the greedy side constraints.
framings.key_insight: This turns the conjecture into a certificate problem. Either one finds explicit witness configurations for long holes, or the solver returns reusable infeasibility certificates that can suggest theorem-grade lemmas.
framings.suggested_technique: Use logic-based Benders decomposition or branch-and-cut with no-good cuts, separating border-choice constraints from interval-coverage constraints and extracting minimal infeasible cores for large-hole instances.
framings.mapping_back: If every attempted hole of length greater than L triggers one of finitely many cut families, those cuts become candidates for a human proof that the greedy table cannot produce larger gaps.

framings.reframing: Regard A_n and B_n as a growing two-color multiplicative generating system inside a commutative monoid. An integer is represented exactly when it admits a factorization with one factor from A_n and one from B_n, so the gap problem asks whether the defect set of this constrained factorization system can contain arbitrarily long runs.
framings.key_insight: This emphasizes that the issue is not generic divisor density but the structure of a very special factorization monoid with two distinguished atom classes. Missing intervals are intervals where all admissible factorizations fail simultaneously.
framings.suggested_technique: Import invariants from factorization theory, such as factorization posets, delta sets, and catenary-style measurements, to quantify how representability changes when a new generator enters one color class.
framings.mapping_back: If the constrained monoid has uniformly controlled factorization transitions, then its defect set cannot develop arbitrarily long consecutive runs, which would imply bounded first-row gaps.
